scores.evidence: so no event is lost or duplicated when the DB commit succeeds
scores.rationale: Technically precise throughout (RLS, SKIP LOCKED, SAQ-A, idempotency), with only a minor overstatement of outbox guarantees (outbox is at-least-once; duplicates are possible downstream), harmless since consumers are idempotent.

scores.evidence: I've assumed you run a SaaS product and need to bill your tenants for subscriptions, usage, seats and add-ons.
scores.rationale: Resolves the request's main ambiguity explicitly, covers all core billing capabilities, phases the work realistically, and explicitly flags build-vs-buy before committing.

scores.evidence: strong (ACID) for invoices, payments, the ledger and subscriptions. Eventual for entitlements, analytics and notifications.
scores.rationale: Components have clear ownership, data flows connect, and cross-cutting choices (tenancy, idempotency, consistency, events via outbox) are applied uniformly; the only loose end is a trivial 5ms vs 10ms entitlement latency mismatch.

scores.evidence: run the new engine alongside the old one and diff every invoice. Ship only when the diff is empty or explained.
scores.rationale: Test clocks, property-based invariants, golden invoices, shadow billing and chaos tests target the real billing failure risks with checkable criteria, but load validation of the 50k events/s ingest and month-start billing spike is missing.

scores.evidence: Target scale for this design: about 10k tenants, about 1M billable accounts, a peak of about 50k usage events per second
scores.rationale: Scale, scope and variant assumptions are explicit and labeled as design targets, estimates are marked approximate, and the plan states how the design changes if the billing-as-a-service assumption differs.

scores.evidence: If ClickHouse is unavailable, billing for usage subscriptions is delayed (with an alert), never billed as zero.
scores.rationale: Covers subtle domain failures — duplicate/out-of-order webhooks, late usage events, crash between finalize and ledger post, non-retryable failure codes, noisy neighbors — each with concrete detection and recovery.

scores.evidence: a daily job matches payments in the ledger against provider settlement reports and payouts... Any mismatch raises an alert and goes to an ops queue.
scores.rationale: Domain-meaningful SLOs, alerting, reconciliation ownership and monolith-first sizing are concrete and plausible for a real team, but deployment, rollback and schema-migration mechanics are not addressed.

scores.evidence: Building billing is a multi-year commitment. The edge cases (tax, proration, dunning, revenue recognition, SCA...) are where most of the effort goes.
scores.rationale: Identifies engineering time as the dominant cost and frames buy options, but gives no treatment of infrastructure/vendor cost scaling with usage, provider fee economics, or any grounded run-cost estimates.

scores.evidence: everything below the Billing Engine sits behind adapters
scores.rationale: Hard-to-reverse choices (tenancy model, ledger, price versioning, provider coupling) get the most care, with explicit exit paths: adapters, monolith-first splitting, cell migration via logical replication, and deferrable build-vs-buy.

scores.evidence: Start with a modular monolith... Split out Usage Ingest and Entitlements first, because their scaling needs are very different.
scores.rationale: Mostly proportionate with a phased growth path, but the Kafka/ClickHouse/Citus/Temporal stack is driven by a self-assumed 50k events/s target and could be simplified for many realistic starting points.

scores.evidence: 1 – MVP (≈3 months): Catalog with versioned prices, accounts, flat and per-seat subscriptions, the billing run, a Stripe adapter...
scores.rationale: Concrete schemas, idempotency-key composition, state machine, drawdown order and a dependency-justified phase order with verifiable artifacts (golden invoices, shadow diffs) let a team start immediately.

checklist.evidence: Store money as an integer in minor units plus an ISO currency code. Never use floats.
Finalized invoices can't be changed. Fix them with credit notes or adjustments.
Make every write idempotent, using idempotency keys on API calls, jobs and webhooks.
card data never touches your servers. Use hosted fields or Elements, store tokens only, and aim for SAQ-A.
Postgres Row-Level Security uses SET app.tenant_id per connection or transaction, as a second guard behind app-level scoping.
Accept events until period_end + grace... Usage that arrives later goes onto the next invoice as an adjustment line tied to the original period.
credit old_amount × unused_fraction, charge new_amount × remaining_fraction. Compute the fraction by seconds, and document that choice
Handle VAT reverse-charge with a validated VAT ID, US sales-tax nexus, and tax-exempt certificates.
retries on days 1, 3, 5 and 7 with smart retry timing. Each retry sends an email asking the customer to update their card.
a daily job matches payments in the ledger against provider settlement reports and payouts, net of fees.
Keep billing and entitlements separate... check "can tenant X use feature Y?" in under 5 ms, without calling billing.
build metering and entitlements yourself... and buy invoicing, payments and tax.

traps.evidence: Store money as an integer in minor units plus an ISO currency code. Never use floats.
Finalized invoices can't be changed. Fix them with credit notes or adjustments.
Inbound webhooks are verified, stored raw, deduplicated by provider_event_id, and processed asynchronously.
card data never touches your servers. Use hosted fields or Elements, store tokens only
tenant_id is on every row and leads every PK and index. Postgres Row-Level Security...

note: An expert-grade billing architecture that avoids every classic trap and nails correctness, failure modes and reversibility; remaining gaps are rounding-rule specifics, deployment/rollback mechanics, scale/load validation, and quantified cost reasoning.
